reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes OneCoin packages as a money-making opportunity, citing projections such as nearly tenfold growth within a year and recovery of the investment in 3.5 to 4.5 months. It also urges donations and partner recruitment, with package volume tied to a percentage-based bonus. The speaker's disclaimer and denial of tricking viewers do not erase these promotional claims and incentives.

opening.argument: Judge the earnings figures as conditional projections, not promises. The speaker calls the near-tenfold scenario a mathematical model and says, “I do not take guarantee.” He also asks viewers to study the project carefully and not enter on emotion. That does not validate the investment, but it matters when deciding whether the presentation asserts a certain return: the speaker expressly puts the decision and its risks on the viewer.

citations.quote: Therefore, you increase your capital by almost ten times, yes, all this during the first year. This, of course, is a mathematical model.
I do not take guarantee
decision about entering into business we accept after careful study of the project Not on the emotions please go into business.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening cites package size, tokens, and bonus qualifications, but none of those quotations establishes that the projected return is guaranteed. The speaker explicitly identifies his calculation as a model and disclaims a guarantee. A conditional forecast can be aggressive without being a promise of a fixed payout.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The disclaimer does not change what viewers are urged to do. After presenting the model, the speaker tells them to make donations and invite partners before the split, then predicts that an investment returns in 3.5 to 4.5 months. Those are concrete purchase and earnings inducements, even if he stops short of a guarantee.

opening.argument: This is also a teaching presentation: the speaker polls the audience about Bitcoin, promises to demonstrate what cryptocurrency is, and describes videos and slides for that purpose. He presents OneCoin Academy as online training in cryptocurrency, investing, and financial literacy. The cited token and package details can therefore be read as an explanation of the system being taught, rather than proof that the educational material itself is a fraudulent transaction.

citations.quote: So, I will briefly demonstrate what cryptocurrency actually is. I will have a couple of short videos, and share the slides too.
We offer training. Teaching on what? Teaching on cryptocurrency, teaching on how to get profits, teaching on investments, financial literacy. Teaching on how to invest in gold.
This's online training.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The quoted right to mine and package amounts identify what the presentation discusses; they do not, alone, settle whether its primary function is solicitation or instruction. The speaker explicitly sets aside time to explain cryptocurrency to an audience with mixed familiarity. The prosecution's reading underweights that substantial explanatory framing.

citations.quote: So, I will briefly demonstrate what cryptocurrency actually is. I will have a couple of short videos, and share the slides too.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The speaker himself limits the training explanation: he says it is formally the product, while participants are mostly buying tokens. He then directly urges viewers to enter before the split and invite partners. The tutorial material serves a paid earnings pitch, not an independent lesson.

citations.quote: Formally, it's the training. The tokens here are free and kinda off the bat, but also, of course, we are mostly buying the tokens by ourselves.
But don't forget that soon is the first split, so make donations, invite partners. Just before the split is now a good moment to enter the business.

opening.argument: The presentation describes a priced training product with token allocations, plus stated rules for handling partner earnings. Those features warrant scrutiny, but the cited presentation is not evidence that a viewer paid and lost money, or that any projected return was actually guaranteed. Even the account explanation distinguishes cash available for withdrawal from a portion used to buy more tokens. Treat the pitch as an offer whose claims need verification, not as proof of a completed deceptive outcome.

rebuttal.rebuttal: A right to mine describes what tokens purportedly confer; the cited package amount is a price, not evidence of a completed loss. The matching-bonus quotation describes a qualification condition, not proof that anyone received an assured return. These specifics support examining the offer closely, but they do not establish a completed deceptive transaction.

citations.quote: Token is a right to mine ONE coin.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A completed loss is not required to assess what the video promotes. The speaker says participants are mostly buying tokens, links larger packages to more coins and profit, and calls for donations and partner invitations before the split. The commercial offer is presented as a route to returns, not merely as training with incidental rewards.
